title: The Adventures of Robin Hood - Take a Look
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BkAhos9qrLQ

Daniel (@dungeondive) admits people are surprised he likes Legends of Andor so much, given how puzzly it is, but it was Michael Menzel's cohesive vision that won him over. So he dives into Menzel's follow-up from Kosmos, The Adventures of Robin Hood, a light co-op that blends storybook and board game. It came at the right time: work stress had him craving something simple.

And it is wonderfully simple. There are no cards, no character sheets and no punchboards, just gorgeous carved wooden meeples, cubes for equipment, and a thick, beautifully bound storybook with two ribbon bookmarks. You learn as you play. Movement uses linked wooden pieces like a little train, you slip from shade to shade to avoid flipped-up guards, and every question mark on Menzel's pastoral board sends you to a storybook page. What he loves most is that the art matters: if you see a cart or a woman in the illustration, you can interact with them. He shows the tutorial chapter, where Little John must escape the castle to meet Robin outside the walls.

His big complaint is the multi-layer board. It warps badly, and its pop-out pieces tear the art when pried up, so his copy is already scarred. That leaves him worried about a similarly built game he's eagerly awaiting. It's a one-and-done (perhaps two-and-done) campaign best shared with family or friends, and he recommends it to Andor fans despite the components.

----

Do multi-layer boards and pop-out tiles add enough to a game to justify the warping and wear, or would you rather they stayed flat?
